DURR-FULL:v5p378/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r4.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r4.claim: Ibn Umar says a connected exception prevents an oath from being broken, while an unconnected one does not.

DURR-FULL:v5p378/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r5.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r5.claim: The Prophet says whoever makes an oath conditional on God's will may carry it out or withdraw without breaking it.

DURR-FULL:v5p378/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r6.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r6.claim: Solomon vowed to visit ninety wives so each would bear a fighter; he forgot the exception despite the angel's reminder, and only one half-formed child was born. The Prophet said the exception would have fulfilled his wish without breaking the oath.

DURR-FULL:v5p378/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r7.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r7.claim: Ikrima interprets remembering one's Lord as remembering while angry.

DURR-FULL:v5p378/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r8.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r8.claim: Hasan explains the verse as referring to when one failed to say إن شاء الله.

DURR-FULL:v5p378/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r9.speaker: أبو الحارث
DURR-FULL:v5p378/r9.claim: A Kufan Quran reciter says that after forgetting God's will, one repents by saying the following prayer for closer guidance.

BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r1.claim: Abū al-Layth transmits via Abū Hurayra that Solomon vowed to visit one hundred wives to have warriors, forgot to say إن شاء الله, and all but one-half of a childless birth failed; the Prophet said the vow would have succeeded had he said it.

BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r2.claim: When people act as if they have independent will, God customarily brings about the opposite to show that only He has true will.

BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r3.claim: A hadith says complete faith includes making an exception in all speech, inwardly as well as outwardly; a merely verbal exception is ineffective.

BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r4.speaker: مولانا
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r4.claim: His couplet says that omitting an exception hardens intention, and the soul—not just passing words—must join the exception.

BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r5.speaker: روضة الخطيب
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r5.claim: A humorous story tells of a man who refused to say إن شاء الله while going to buy a donkey, lost his money, and later described the loss with repeated exceptions.

BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r6.claim: He permitted a delayed exception based on this verse, while most jurists rejected that rule because it would unsettle confessions, divorce, emancipation, and reports about the future.

BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r7.speaker: القرطبي
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r7.claim: The verse allows a delayed exception to retract and escape sin, but an exception changing a legal ruling must be connected to the original statement.

BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r8.speaker: أبو حنيفة
BURSEVI:v5p181#2/r8.claim: At al-Manṣūr's court, Abū Ḥanīfa ruled an exception after a pause to an oath ineffective; Ibn Isḥāq appealed to Ibn ʿAbbās's view, but Abū Ḥanīfa explained its valid interpretation and warned that broad use could let people evade allegiance. Al-Manṣūr imprisoned Ibn Isḥāq.

BURSEVI:v5p181/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p181/r1.claim: A future commitment is permissible only while conditioned on God's will; inwardly, choices and deeds all depend on God's will. When the qualification is remembered, one should say إن شاء الله.

BURSEVI:v5p181/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v5p181/r2.claim: A report says the Prophet said إن شاء الله when the revelation arrived after his lapse.

BURSEVI:v5p181/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p181/r3.claim: He asks God for a clearer sign than the Cave youths' story as proof of prophethood; God gave him even more evident signs in distant prophetic histories and future events to the end of time.

BURSEVI:v5p181/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181/r4.speaker: سعدي المفتي
BURSEVI:v5p181/r4.claim: Since the Jews made the Cave story evidence for Muhammad's prophethood, God diminished its importance with this wording, as at the chapter's opening.

BURSEVI:v5p181/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181/r5.speaker: السمرقندي
BURSEVI:v5p181/r5.claim: Another reading says that when someone forgets a thing, he should remember God and ask to be guided to something else that is closer, better, and more beneficial.

BURSEVI:v5p181/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p181/r6.speaker: الإمام
BURSEVI:v5p181/r6.claim: One may die before tomorrow or be obstructed while alive; without conditioning a promise on God's will, failure would be a lie, repugnant and unfitting for prophets.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r1.speaker: ابن عطية
ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya, following al-Tabari's rebuttal, calls the exception for God's will corrupt; Alusi says this is unfair and the exception properly attaches to the prohibition.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r2.speaker: الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r2.claim: The exception can mean do not say it in any state except while mentioning God's will, since a spoken promise cannot literally be joined to the divine will; another analysis makes it a state exception with an elided bāʾ.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r3.claim: The exception may instead refer to times, with God's will interpreted as permission: do not speak until God authorizes it; it may also be a disconnected exception signaling a permanent prohibition because the time of God's will is unknown.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r4.claim: The permanent-prohibition reading is not that God never wills the Prophet to speak because such speech is intrinsically bad; limiting the rule to revelation still does not follow from the text's indefinite noun under negation.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p247#3/r5.claim: The apparent reading attaches the exception to the prohibition, and the Prophet's community is included in the address; it cannot sensibly attach to the declaration that he will act, because either proposed sense conflicts with the prohibition.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r1.speaker: الخفاجي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r1.claim: Al-Khafaji rejects attaching the exception to nonperformance: Sunnis and Muʿtazilites alike cannot make that a coherent prohibition, since God can prevent an intended act through death or another impediment.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r10.speaker: الراغب
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r10.claim: Al-Rāghib defines exception as removing what a preceding general statement entails, as in the verse about what may be eaten, or what a particular utterance entails, as in a conditional divorce.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r11.claim: The Prophetic report says that whoever swears to something and says if God wills has made an exception; al-Ālūsī therefore rejects explanations that call the phrase an exception only because of its Quranic wording or resemblance.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r12.claim: Remembering the Lord means remembering His will, with an omitted genitive; the preceding command is to say if God wills, as the Prophet did when this verse came down.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r13.claim: Forgetting means an inadvertent omission; the command applies upon remembering, not during forgetfulness, and requires recovery whether the interval is short or long.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r14.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r14.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās held that a person may add the exception even after a year; this is also reported from the Imams of the Prophet's family and as one narration from Aḥmad.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r15.speaker: ابن جبير
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r15.claim: Ibn Jubayr says a person who swore and forgot to except retains the right of exception for a month.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r16.speaker: عطاء
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r16.claim: ʿAṭāʾ, reporting from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, allows the exception for as long as it takes to milk a camel.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r17.speaker: طاوس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r17.claim: Ṭāwūs limits the exception to the time a person remains in the same sitting.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r18.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r18.speaker: إبراهيم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r18.claim: Ibrāhīm says the exception is available only while the person is still speaking.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r19.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r19.speaker: عامة الفقهاء
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r19.claim: Most jurists require the exception to be connected to the oath; allowing it after any delay would undermine the finality of acknowledgments, divorce, emancipation, and truthful or false statements.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r2.speaker: الخفاجي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r2.claim: He also rejects reading the verse as forbidding a Muʿtazilite to claim independent authorship whenever God's will does not accompany the act.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r20.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r20.speaker: أبو حنيفة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r20.claim: In a story, Abū Ḥanīfa answers al-Manṣūr's objection to his disagreement with Ibn ʿAbbās by warning that delayed exceptions would let people leave a pledge of allegiance and then break it; al-Manṣūr approves the answer.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r3.speaker: الاعتراض على المعتزلة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r3.claim: A familiar objection says that if God wills only obedience, a debtor who vows to pay tomorrow if God wills must be perjured when he fails to pay, making the exception ineffective; it is like a condition whose condition occurs.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r4.speaker: المرتضى
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r4.claim: Al-Murtaḍā distinguishes exceptions that suspend the legal force of oaths, contracts, and reports; this use may be retrospective but is unsuitable for sins because it displays reliance on God.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r5.speaker: المرتضى
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r5.claim: A second use in permitted matters asks God to enable the act and preserve the existing state; al-Murtaḍā considers this possible in the verse.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r6.speaker: المرتضى
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r6.claim: A third use merely expresses reliance on God without deciding whether the statement is true or false, and could also fit the verse.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r7.speaker: المرتضى
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r7.claim: A fourth use seeks divine grace and facilitation, which applies only to obedience and cannot explain the verse's broader scope; if the debtor intended another sense, he need not be perjured.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r8.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the objection and this answer are unpersuasive, and the Muʿtazilite position can be refuted without them.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r9.speaker: السيرافي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p248/r9.claim: Using exception for qualification by saying if God wills, and for qualification by a condition generally, is established in Arabic usage.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r1.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r1.claim: One interpretation makes remembering the Lord mean glorifying and seeking forgiveness after forgetting the exception, urging it by implying that its omission merits repentance.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r2.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r2.claim: Another reads the command as remembering God and His punishment after leaving an instruction, to prompt correction; forgetfulness here is figurative for leaving something.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r3.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r3.claim: A further reading says to remember God when forgetfulness comes so He may remind the person of what was forgotten; it treats forgetfulness as intransitive, but connects poorly to the context.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r4.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r4.claim: Qatāda takes the verse to command making up a missed prayer when one remembers it; al-Ālūsī says this seems to be his intended reading and has the same weak contextual connection.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r5.claim: If Qatāda instead infers prayer's make-up from the command to remember a forgotten exception, the analogy is more plausible because prayer merits greater concern, though this is not the apparent report.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r6.speaker: عكرمة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r6.claim: ʿIkrima interprets the verse as remembering God when angry, since anger can cause forgetfulness; al-Ālūsī regards its contextual problem as like the prior interpretations.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r7.speaker: الزجاج
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r7.claim: Al-Zajjāj reads the prayer for guidance as asking God to grant a sign more evident than the account of the Companions of the Cave, proving the Prophet's mission and guiding people.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r8.claim: God later gave the Prophet clearer signs, including accounts of distant prophets and future events through the Resurrection; the wording also gently reduces the cave story's apparent wonder, as did the opening question.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r9.speaker: بعض الأفاضل
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250#2/r9.claim: One syntactic proposal links the prayer for guidance back to the command to recall when the youths took refuge in the cave: tell that story and hope for a clearer sign.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r1.claim: A traveler from the Maghrib hears two Baghdad vegetable sellers debate delayed exceptions: one argues that Job would have been told to except if Ibn ʿAbbās were right, since the remedy in the verse about his oath came after a year.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r2.claim: The traveler returns home impressed that even a street seller could challenge Ibn ʿAbbās, and infers how learned Baghdad's scholars must be.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r3.claim: Al-Ālūsī says such an objection is excessive even from a vegetable seller and cautions that God knows whether the anecdote is authentic.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r4.claim: The apparent verse and report may seem to support Ibn ʿAbbās, but the required recovery is only a renewed declaration of dependence on God, not a delayed change to legal effect; the passage does not address legal rulings.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r5.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that one who forgot the exception should make it when remembering, but that this privilege belongs only to the Prophet; others may except only as part of an oath.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r6.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p250/r6.claim: An alternative says the later words attach to an implied recurring statement: whenever one forgets God, remember Him upon recollection, or say if God wills when announcing a future act; al-Ālūsī finds this far from the apparent sense.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r1.speaker: الجبائي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r1.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī links the guidance prayer to remembering God: ask God to remind the Prophet of a forgotten matter, and if not, to guide him to something nearer and more beneficial; al-Ālūsī finds this closer syntactically but distant in other respects.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r2.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r2.claim: Another proposal links it to the preceding commands and prohibitions: hope for guidance to what is more beneficial than their instruction; al-Ālūsī judges this strained.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r3.speaker: ابن الأنباري
ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r3.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī says God may reveal answers to the questioners before the promised time and hasten guidance; al-Ālūsī says the meaning cannot be derived and would make the Quran like a riddle.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r4.speaker: رجل من أهل الكوفة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p251/r4.claim: An unnamed Kufan, transmitted through Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān and his father and attributed by Abū Ḥayyān to Muḥammad al-Kūfī, says repentance for forgetting the exception is to recite the guidance prayer; al-Ālūsī says it has no evidence.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p261/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p261/r1.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p261/r1.claim: An esoteric interpretation says to remember God after forgetting the whole universe, including oneself, because remembrance becomes pure only then.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p261/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p261/r2.speaker: الجنيد
ALUSI-FULL:v15p261/r2.claim: Al-Junayd reads the command as remembering after forgetting remembrance itself; true remembrance is annihilation in the Remembered apart from the act of remembering.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p261/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p261/r3.speaker: الجنيد
ALUSI-FULL:v15p261/r3.claim: Al-Junayd says a station above remembrance is nearer to guidance: God describes and remembers the servant before the servant remembers Him.

ELMALILI:18:23/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:23/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:23/r2.claim: If one forgets to say “if God wills,” one should remember God when recalling it, by saying it then or by glorification and seeking forgiveness; this expiates the lapse even if it does not change the statement's effect.

ELMALILI:18:23/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:23/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:23/r3.claim: An alternative reading is that remembering God after forgetting anything acknowledges human weakness and may help one recall the forgotten thing.

ELMALILI:18:24-26/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:24-26/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:24-26/r1.claim: The prayer asks that the Lord bring the Prophet to success more directly than the Cave companions' success.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes ‘unless God wills’ as an exception from the prohibition itself: one may make the statement only if God permits it, with the omitted object supplied from context.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r2.speaker: الكسائي والأخفش والفراء
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r2.claim: Al-Kisāʾī, al-Akhfash, and al-Farrāʾ take the exception from ‘I will do that tomorrow’: the promise is allowed when accompanied by saying ‘if God wills.’

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r3.claim: The verse honors the Prophet by answering his question, teaching prophetic etiquette, and postponing the rebuke until after answering so he would not mistake correction for refusal.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r4.speaker: حكيم بن حزام
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295#2/r4.claim: In a report, the Prophet gave Ḥakīm repeatedly when he asked, then advised him about taking wealth freely; Ḥakīm understood the counsel was ethical and vowed not to take from anyone else.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r1.speaker: ابن إسحاق والطبري والواحدي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r1.claim: Reports say the polytheists asked about the sleepers and Dhū al-Qarnayn, and the Prophet promised an answer the next day without saying ‘if God wills’; revelation was delayed fifteen days, or three in another report.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r2.claim: Ibn Ashur treats the delayed revelation as a subtle reproach, followed by a direct prohibition against promising future action without qualifying it by God’s will.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r3.speaker: البخاري
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r3.claim: Bukhari’s report about Solomon says he vowed to visit one hundred women in a night so each would bear a fighter, but only one gave birth to half a boy.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p295/r4.claim: The Prophet forgot to say ‘if God wills’ when promising an answer; after relating the story, God forbade unqualified promises, as with Solomon’s forgotten qualification.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r1.claim: The lām in li-shayʾ is causal, meaning ‘for something you intend to do’; dhālika refers to that intended action, including answering their question.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r2.claim: Ghadā is a figurative term for future time, not necessarily the next day, as in Zuhayr’s contrast among today, yesterday, and tomorrow.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r3.claim: Although the apparent scope is future plans, most jurists say adding ‘if God wills’ releases an oath without expiation; they extend the broad wording to vows.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r4.speaker: ابن القاسم وأشهب وابن عبد الحكم عن مالك
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r4.claim: These transmit from Mālik that ‘remember your Lord when you forget’ concerns remembering God after forgetfulness, not oath exceptions; the oath ruling comes from Sunna, as also held by Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r5.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p297/r5.claim: ʿUmar says the best remembrance of God is to remember Him when encountering His commands and prohibitions, supporting the meaning of remembrance as compliance.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r1.claim: Addressing God as ‘your Lord’ rather than using the divine name carries a special gentleness; the object of forgetting is the prohibition just mentioned.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r2.claim: Some jurists read ‘remember your Lord when you forget’ as permission to add an oath exception upon remembering, without a time limit; Ibn ʿAbbās permits even a long delay.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r3.claim: The majority reject using this verse to permit delayed oath exceptions, arguing that the Sunna states otherwise.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r4.claim: After fulfilling the promised answer about the sleepers, God rebukes the Prophet for engaging questions beyond the mission without permission and directs him to seek more important guidance in revealed law.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r5.claim: ‘Say, perhaps my Lord will guide me’ may continue the command not to dispute their number, or be a prayer joined to remembering God after forgetting.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p298/r6.claim: Rushdan either specifies the comparative relation in ‘closer than this’ or serves as an absolute object describing the kind of guidance sought.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r1.claim: Because the command continues the prior instruction, forgetting means forgetting the exception; remembering God means restoring awareness that He owns and empowers the act.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r2.claim: When one remembers the omission, append the exception before finishing, repeat the statement afterward, or hold the intention and add it later; any remembrance of God’s authority is suitable.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r3.claim: Some reports say that when the verses were revealed, the Prophet added the words if God wills.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r4.claim: The author rejects readings that the verse independently commands remembering God after forgetting Him or anything else, and readings that require only a fixed formula or repentance.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#25/r5.claim: The phrase hoping for nearer guidance refers to moving from remembering after an omission to constant remembrance without forgetting.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#26/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#26/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#26/r1.claim: Regularly remembering something after forgetting it helps establish continuous remembrance, as the call to remember God morning and evening illustrates.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#26/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#26/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#26/r2.claim: The author calls it mistaken to take this as a request for further signs that guide people better than the Cave story; the context concerns remembrance after forgetting the exception.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#26/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#26/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#26/r3.claim: Other proposed readings refer this to the forgotten object, ask God to restore it, or treat the next clause as an explanatory repentance formula; the author says all depend on the wrong sense of forgetting.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r1.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:9-26#27/r1.claim: The Prophet promised answers the next day without saying if God wills; revelation stopped for forty days, causing grief and doubt while Quraysh mocked, then Gabriel explained revelation comes only by God’s permission.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r8.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r8.claim: An account from ʿAlī says a person swearing by God may make an exception for forty days, recalling the Prophet’s delayed answer to Jewish questioners after he omitted “if God wills.”

TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r9.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r9.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī defines thunyā as an exception and says related reports suggest a decisive oath; whether an exception can qualify an already binding oath is left to jurisprudence.

ASAD-NOTES:18:23#n33/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:23#n33/r1.speaker: almost all of the commentators
ASAD-NOTES:18:23#n33/r1.claim: Commentators say the passage first addresses the Prophet after he promised Quraysh an answer about the Cave story the next day and revelation was then withheld as disapproval.

ASAD-NOTES:18:23#n33/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:23#n33/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:23#n33/r2.claim: The exhortation also states a general principle for all believers.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The Prophet was told not to promise an answer for the next day on his own; he may have done so when asked about the cave-dwellers, whose questioners were testing him.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The Prophet eagerly wanted to answer every objection to vindicate his message, but divine wisdom may defer or withhold an answer, so promises must be conditional on God's will.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: God's wisdom can delay or withhold an answer; the Prophet should condition every promise on God's will and, if he forgets, remember God when he recalls it.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: After remembering God, the Prophet may tell those he promised that his Lord may guide him to the right answer before the promised time.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:23/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:23/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:23/r1.claim: When asked about the Cave story, the Prophet promised an answer the next day without saying ‘if God wills’; revelation paused for a time, then came after fifteen days with a warning.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:23/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:23/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:23/r2.claim: No one knows what they will do tomorrow, and human intention alone cannot bring an event about without God’s will.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:23/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:23/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:23/r3.claim: It is commendable to qualify future intentions by God’s will; the common Turkish expression inşallah matches the verse, as does the phrase in several other verses.

QIRAAT-ER:18:24:14#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:24:14#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:24:14#1/r1.claim: The full first-person yāʾ is retained in the standard form.

QIRAAT-ER:18:24:14#2/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:18:24:14#2/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:18:24:14#2/r1.claim: The pausal form has nūn sākina, while connected reading retains full yahdiyanī.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r3.claim: The instruction to say tomorrow fits the occasion: when asked three questions, including about the Cave youths, the Prophet promised an answer the next day, but revelation was delayed fifteen nights and rumors spread.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r4.claim: The occasion does not limit the verse to one case; the parallel command about coercing women addressed Abdullah ibn Ubayy's attempt to force women who wanted chastity, while other texts clarify the broader issue.

STUDYQURAN:18:23/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r1.claim: The verses address the Prophet: do not promise future action, using tomorrow for the future generally, without making fulfillment conditional on God’s will.

STUDYQURAN:18:23/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r10.speaker: Bḍ, JJ, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r10.claim: Another reading makes it the Prophet’s prayer for signs and proofs of prophethood even greater than the information about the Cave youths.

STUDYQURAN:18:23/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r2.claim: The context is Muhammad’s promise to answer Meccan questions about the youths the next day; revelation was delayed fifteen days, prompting doubts about his answer and prophethood.

STUDYQURAN:18:23/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r3.speaker: some commentators
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r3.claim: Some commentators read this as an instruction to say “if God wills” with any promise about future action.

STUDYQURAN:18:23/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r4.claim: Muslims commonly say in shāʾ Allāh about future aims, recalling that nothing lies outside God’s will and the future is in His hands.

STUDYQURAN:18:23/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r5.claim: If the Prophet forgets to acknowledge God’s will, he and all people should remember God again; this calls for recollection rather than regret and resembles 6:68.

STUDYQURAN:18:23/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r6.speaker: JJ, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r6.claim: Some say one should correct the omission while still in the place and situation where the original statement was made.

STUDYQURAN:18:23/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r7.speaker: Ṭ, Z
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r7.claim: Others allow saying the formula much later, though one may then owe expiation for an unfulfilled oath.

STUDYQURAN:18:23/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r8.claim: The expiation discussion points to Quranic instructions on keeping and breaking oaths.

STUDYQURAN:18:23/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r9.speaker: Z
STUDYQURAN:18:23/r9.claim: One reading takes the request for nearer rectitude as the words to say when remembering the forgotten acknowledgment of God’s will.

STUDYQURAN:18:intro/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:intro/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:intro/r6.claim: After promising an answer the next day, the Prophet waited fifteen days without revelation; v. 6 reproaches his concern about Quraysh's disbelief, and vv. 23–24 warn against future promises without invoking God's will.
